title: Review: Uncertainties and errors; Graphs and data analysis; Density; Springs and Hooke's law; Stress–strain and force–extension behaviour; Stress, strain and Young modulus
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: D06-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; FL01-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; MS03-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; D06-1#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: D06-1#N.12, FL01-1#N.4, MS02-1#N.11, MT01-1#N.6, D06-1#N.2b, MS02-1#N.5, MT01-1#N.8, MS02-1#N.3, MT01-1#N.9. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Extension
items.clue: Stretched length minus the original length, not the whole length.

items.label: Density
items.clue: Mass per unit volume; it belongs to the material, not to the object.

items.label: Gradient
items.clue: Δy divided by Δx, taken from a large triangle; it has its own units.

items.label: Compression
items.clue: Squashing a spring, where the change counted is the decrease in length.

questions.stem: A spring that obeys Hooke's law is 15.0 cm long when it supports a 3.0 N load and 18.0 cm long when it supports a 6.0 N load. What is its natural (unloaded) length?

options.text: 0 cm

questions.explanation: The extra 3.0 N adds 3.0 cm, so the extension is 1.0 cm per newton. With 3.0 N on, the extension is 3.0 cm: natural length = 15.0 − 3.0 = 12.0 cm.

questions.stem: The density of aluminium is 2.7 g cm⁻³. What is the volume, in m³, of an aluminium block of mass 0.081 kg?

A student measures the diameter of a wire five times with a micrometer: 0.55, 0.56, 0.55, 0.55, 0.56 mm. Later she notices that the micrometer reads 0.03 mm when fully closed. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The readings are accurate, because they agree closely with each other.
Taking more readings and averaging them would remove the error.
The readings are precise but not accurate; subtract 0.03 mm from each.
The error is random, so a micrometer with a finer resolution is needed.

questions.explanation: Small spread means precise. The zero error is systematic: correct it by subtracting the zero reading, giving about 0.52–0.53 mm.

questions.stem: A student repeats the Young modulus experiment with the same loads on a wire of the same metal and diameter, but only one tenth as long. The extension is read with the same scale. What is the main effect?

options.text: Each extension is ten times smaller, so its percentage uncertainty is ten times larger.
The Young modulus found is ten times smaller.
The stress is ten times larger, so the wire passes its limit of proportionality.
Nothing changes, as the Young modulus is a property of the material.

questions.explanation: Strain is unchanged, so extension ∝ original length. The same reading error is now ten times larger as a fraction of the extension.

questions.stem: In a lab, a student models a spring as a light spring that obeys Hooke's law. Which statement describes how the spring's force behaves in this model?

options.text: Its force is proportional to its length, measured end to end.
Its force doubles when its extension doubles.
Its force is the same however far it is stretched or compressed.
Its force depends on how fast the attached object is moving.

questions.stem: A ball's fall is timed four times: 0.62 s, 0.57 s, 0.65 s, 0.60 s. The stopwatch reads to 0.01 s. Which is the best way to write the result?
questions.explanation: Mean = 2.44 ÷ 4 = 0.61 s. Half the range = (0.65 − 0.57) ÷ 2 = 0.04 s. The scatter is far bigger than the resolution, so it sets the uncertainty.

questions.stem: A cable must carry 12 kN. Steel: working stress 200 MPa, density 7850 kg m⁻³, £1.00 per kg. Aluminium alloy: working stress 100 MPa, density 2700 kg m⁻³, £2.50 per kg. Each cable is made with the smallest safe area. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Aluminium is cheaper and lighter, as it is less dense.
Steel is both cheaper and lighter, as it is stronger.
Steel is cheaper per metre; aluminium is lighter per metre.
They cost the same, as each is used at its own working stress.

questions.explanation: Steel: area = 12 × 10³ ÷ 2.0 × 10⁸ = 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ m², mass 0.47 kg per metre, £0.47. Aluminium: area 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ m², 0.32 kg per metre, £0.81.

questions.stem: A student times a trolley rolling down a ramp with a hand-held stopwatch that reads to 0.01 s. Her five times vary by about 0.2 s. Which change would most reduce the effect of this random error on her result?

options.text: Use a stopwatch that reads to 0.001 s instead of 0.01 s.
Check that the stopwatch reads zero before each timing.
Subtract her typical reaction time from each reading.
Time the run with light gates and an electronic timer.

questions.explanation: The varying human reaction is the source of the scatter. Automatic timing removes it.

questions.stem: Two cables are made of the same aluminium alloy and carry the same load. Cable Q is 3 times as long as cable P and has 3 times its diameter. Both obey Hooke's law. What is the extension of Q divided by the extension of P?
questions.explanation: Extension = force × length ÷ (area × Young modulus). Same force and material; length × 3; area × 3² = 9. Ratio = 3/9 = 1/3.
